title: The Derivative: the ring, the circle, the point

segments.text: Put a point under a microscope. Around it is a tiny ring of directions. Watch where the function sends that ring. If it comes out as a ring that is only turned and stretched, by one number, then up close the function is one move.

That number is the derivative, and it is a complex number. So it has two addresses, like any other. In Cartesian it is u sub x plus i times v sub x. In polar, its length is the local stretch and its angle is the local turn.

Here is the test. Take the quotient from every direction. Each direction gives a dot, and the dots trace a circle. Its centre is the move part, A. Its radius is the size of the mirror part, B. The derivative exists exactly when the circle is one point.

Conjugation is pure mirror, so its circle never shrinks. The real part squashes the plane, and its circle has radius one half. But z squared plus z has no mirror at all. Its circle is a point, and the derivative is two z plus one.

Now try the absolute value of z, squared. Its circle has radius equal to the length of z, centred on the mirror image of z. It shrinks to a point only at zero. So it is differentiable at zero, and nowhere else.

In x and y, no mirror part reads: u sub x equals v sub y, and u sub y equals minus v sub x. That is Cauchy-Riemann. Test e to the x, times the quantity cos y plus i sin y. Both hold everywhere, so it is entire, and its derivative is itself. In polar, it stretches by e to the x and turns by y.
